title: Manage a complete attempt and an independent check
chapter: Choose a strategy, then learn from the decision
goal: Keep a clear trail while solving, and check with a different method.

scenes.visual: A page of scattered calculations beside a page with three labelled lines: "known", "cases done", "next".
scenes.narration: Good working leaves a trail. If you write what you have established, which cases you have finished, and what you will do next, you can pause, return, or find a mistake without starting again.

scenes.visual: A clock with time running; a half-finished solution being picked up again smoothly.
scenes.narration: Under time pressure, people lose marks by repeating work or by trusting an answer they never checked. A clear trail and one independent check prevent both.

scenes.visual: A 5 by 5 grid of unit squares with its border squares shaded. Question: "How many squares are on the border?"
scenes.narration: A five by five grid of small squares has all the squares along its border shaded. How many squares are shaded? Pause and find the answer in one way, then in a second, different way.

scenes.visual: Method one: the whole 5 by 5 grid (25) with the inner 3 by 3 block (9) lifted out. 25 minus 9 gives 16.
scenes.narration: First method: take away the inside. The whole grid has twenty-five squares. The unshaded inner block is three by three: nine squares. Twenty-five minus nine is sixteen.

scenes.visual: Method two: four strips of 4 squares each, arranged pinwheel-fashion round the border so that they do not overlap. 4 times 4 gives 16.
scenes.narration: Second method: split the border into four strips of four squares, each strip starting at a corner and stopping one short of the next. Four times four is sixteen. The two methods agree.

scenes.visual: A tempting wrong method: four sides of 5 gives 20, with each corner square flashing as counted twice. 20 minus 4 gives 16.
scenes.narration: A common error is to say four sides of five squares: twenty. That counts each corner twice. Subtract the four corners and you get sixteen again. A second method is valuable precisely because it would have caught that mistake.

scenes.visual: A working page with the three labelled lines filled in for a longer problem; one case ticked, one marked "to do".
scenes.narration: For longer problems, label your cases as you go, and tick each one when it is finished. If you must leave a problem, write one line saying what to do next. Your future self will thank you.

scenes.visual: Lines: "Write what is known and what is next", "Tick off finished cases", "Check with a different method".
scenes.narration: Record what you know and what comes next. Tick off finished cases. Then check the answer by a method that could not make the same mistake. Notebook challenge: find the number of border squares of a seven by seven grid in two different ways.

notebook_exercise: Find the number of border squares of a 7 by 7 grid in two different ways.
